rationale: A wins because it keeps the finance number honest and treats missing proof as a blocker, not decorative seasoning. Its line "what 'annualized revenue' actually means here (ARR, run-rate from a single strong month, GAAP revenue?)" is exactly the discipline this update needs; B walks into the rake with "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth — unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing." ARR and unaudited are not in the facts. B has usable shapes, but it keeps upgrading ambiguity into certainty, which is how a decent angle becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: The third angle overstates the monetization story before the facts support it: "giving the model away to sell everything around it" and "the model is the loss leader" are plausible, not proven.
"Is open-source the new enterprise-AI land grab?" is a shopworn trend wrapper unless A can supply the comparable vendor proof it admits it needs.
A underplays the self-reported benchmark issue as a standalone accountability angle; "benchmark numbers are the company's own" is more than hygiene, it is a real reporter pressure point.
gaps_in_B: B repeatedly converts "annualized revenue" into "ARR" in lines like "$3B ARR says that's a strategy" and "Databricks claims $3B ARR." That is not a synonym you get to assume.
"Unaudited" is invented. The update says Databricks is private and the benchmarks are company-run; it does not say the revenue figure is unaudited.
"Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" plus "data residency" and "audit logging" adds compliance specifics the update did not provide.
The platform-economics angle asserts "the data layer" and "enterprise support" are where the money is, then quietly asks for proof. Lead with that only after you have the exec or analyst on record.
